title: The Atomists
orientation: Russell presents Leucippus and Democritus, the founders of ancient atomism, as producing a theory of matter 'remarkably like that of modern science' and the last major pre-Socratic system free of the 'undue emphasis on man' that Russell thinks afflicts later Greek philosophy. The chapter covers their biographies, the theory of atoms and the void, its role as an answer to Parmenides, a long digression tracing the philosophical history of the void/space problem down to Newton, Leibniz, and Einstein, and Democritus's physics, epistemology, and ethics.
historical_background: Leucippus, from Miletus, flourished around 440 (or, by another estimate, 430) B.C. and was influenced by Parmenides and Zeno; so little is known of him that some ancient and modern writers have doubted his existence, though Aristotle's textual quotations from him make this unlikely. Democritus, a much better-documented figure, was born at Abdera in Thrace, was young when Anaxagoras was old (so flourishing around 420 B.C.), travelled widely (Egypt, Persia) before settling in Abdera. He was a contemporary of Socrates and the Sophists but is treated before them because his thought is inseparable from Leucippus's and because part of his philosophy answers his fellow-townsman Protagoras. Unlike Protagoras, who was welcomed in Athens, Democritus said 'I went to Athens, and no one knew me'; Plato never mentions him and reportedly wished his books burnt, while Aristotle, also an Ionian, knew his work well.
philosophical_problems: How can Parmenides's argument that 'what is' is unchanging be reconciled with the obvious fact of motion and change?
Does motion require the existence of empty space (a void), and if 'nothing' (the void) is not-being, how can it be said to exist?
Should natural phenomena be explained mechanistically (by prior causes) or teleologically (by purpose/final cause)?
What is the status of sensory qualities (warmth, taste, colour) versus supposedly 'real' properties (weight, density, hardness)?
Can an infinite causal chain, or the universe as a whole, have or need an ultimate cause or purpose?

philosophers_discussed.name: Leucippus
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Co-founder of atomism, credited by Russell with the fundamental ideas of the system; from Miletus, influenced by Parmenides and Zeno; sought to reconcile Parmenidean monism with the reality of motion and plurality by positing atoms and the void.

philosophers_discussed.name: Democritus
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Co-founder of atomism and the chapter's more fully documented figure; worked out the theory in detail, applying it to cosmology, biology, perception, and ethics, and held a materialist, deterministic, and religiously sceptical worldview centered on cheerfulness as the goal of life.

philosophers_discussed.name: Parmenides
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: His arguments against not-being (against the void) and for an unchanging, undivided reality are the problem the atomists set out to answer; Russell frames Leucippus's whole project as reconciling Parmenides's logic with the fact of motion.

philosophers_discussed.name: Empedocles
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Represents pluralism, the other pole (with Parmenides's monism) that Leucippus's atomism attempts to mediate between.

philosophers_discussed.name: Epicurus
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: A later follower of Democritus who adopted the view that atoms were originally falling under weight, with heavier atoms overtaking lighter ones, a view Russell judges 'rather unintelligent' compared to the random-motion interpretation he favors for Leucippus and Democritus.

philosophers_discussed.name: Aristotle
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Main ancient source for the atomists' views (quoting Leucippus directly); also criticized them for not accounting for the atoms' original motion, a criticism Russell rejects as misplaced.

philosophers_discussed.name: Newton
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Russell traces the atomists' implicit commitment to absolute space forward to Newton's theory of absolute space, distinguishing absolute from relative motion, as the 'logical development' of the atomist view.

philosophers_discussed.name: Descartes
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Represents the alternative to Newton and Leucippus: that extension is the essence of matter, so there is matter everywhere and empty space is impossible.

philosophers_discussed.name: Leibniz
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Believed, against Newton, that space is merely a system of relations, not a substance; his controversy with Newton (via Clarke) is said by Russell to be settled decisively in Leibniz's favor by Einstein.

core_concepts.name: Atomism (atoms and the void)
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Leucippus and Democritus held that everything in the universe is made of tiny, indestructible, physically unsplittable particles called atoms, moving in empty space (the void), differing only in shape, size, and arrangement.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The theory that all things are composed of an infinite number of atoms, physically (though not geometrically) indivisible, indestructible, always in motion, differing in shape and size, moving through empty space (the void) between them, with observable qualities arising from the arrangement, motion, and collision of atoms rather than from any inherent purpose.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell repeatedly calls it 'the theory of the atomists' the ancient system 'more nearly that of modern science than any other theory propounded in antiquity,' making it a pivotal moment where Greek philosophy anticipates, without the empirical grounding of, later physics and chemistry.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Devised by Leucippus, developed in detail by Democritus, as an attempt to reconcile Parmenides's monism with Empedocles's pluralism and with the observed fact of change.
examples: Fire composed of small spherical atoms
The soul composed of atoms similar to those of fire
Vortices of colliding atoms forming worlds
objections: Aristotle and others reproached the atomists for not accounting for the atoms' original motion.
It was common in antiquity to accuse the atomists of attributing everything to chance (a charge Russell says is mistaken, since they were strict determinists).
competing_positions: Anaxagoras's explanation of vortex-formation via mind, which the atomists replace with a purely mechanical account
Parmenides's denial that not-being (the void) can exist at all
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Revived by Epicurus in antiquity and, Russell notes, revived again in modern times to explain the facts of chemistry, more than two thousand years after Leucippus and Democritus first proposed it without that empirical support.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Underpins Democritus's disbelief in popular religion and his rejection of purpose (Providence) in the universe.

core_concepts.name: The void as a response to Parmenides
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Parmenides argued nothingness (empty space) cannot exist, because saying it 'is' contradicts calling it 'nothing.' The atomists admitted this logical problem but insisted on the void anyway, because motion is an observed fact and, they held, motion is impossible without empty space to move into.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The atomists' response to the Parmenidean argument that not-being cannot be said to exist: they conceded no logical refutation of Parmenides's position but asserted the void as a necessary postulate on empirical grounds, since a plenum (a universe completely full of matter, as Parmenides held) was believed by all parties in this debate to make motion impossible.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: This is the central logical/metaphysical move of the chapter, and Russell uses it to launch a long historical excursus tracing the concept of space through Aristotle, Newton, Descartes, Leibniz, and Einstein.
core_concepts.historical_origin: A direct response to Parmenides's arguments against not-being, reinforced (paradoxically) by the discovery that ostensibly empty containers actually hold air.
examples: Leucippus's own formula: 'The void is a not-being, and no part of what is is a not-being...'
objections: The Parmenidean position, as Russell restates it: 'You say there is the void; therefore the void is not nothing; therefore it is not the void.' Russell says the atomists never really answered this, but simply proclaimed they would ignore it because motion is a fact of experience.
competing_positions: Descartes's plenum theory (extension is the essence of matter, so there is matter everywhere)
Leibniz's relational theory of space (no substantial space or void, only a system of relations)
Newton's absolute space, which Russell calls the 'logical development' of the atomists' implicit view
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Traced by Russell all the way to the Newton-Leibniz-Clarke controversy over absolute versus relative space, which he says Einstein's theory decisively settled in Leibniz's favor, and to modern physics, where empty space is replaced by fields such as light-waves.

core_concepts.name: Mechanistic versus teleological explanation
core_concepts.plain_explanation: There are two different questions we can ask about why something happens: 'What earlier event caused it?' (mechanistic) and 'What purpose does it serve?' (teleological). The atomists asked only the first question, which Russell says is the one that actually leads to scientific knowledge.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell's distinction between mechanistic explanation, which answers 'what earlier circumstances caused this event,' and teleological (final-cause) explanation, which answers 'what purpose did this event serve'; the atomists, unlike Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle after them, sought to explain the world without invoking purpose or final causes.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell treats this as one of the most consequential methodological choices in the history of science: the atomists' mechanistic approach anticipates the method that 'experience has shown' leads to scientific knowledge, while the teleological approach dominant from Socrates through Aristotle 'led science up a blind alley' until the Renaissance.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Framed by Russell as the atomists' distinctive contribution, in contrast to the purpose-driven explanations later associated with Socrates, Plato, and especially Aristotle.
examples: Why does the baker make bread? Because people will be hungry (teleological). What earlier circumstances caused this event? (mechanistic)
objections: Neither kind of question, Russell argues, can be intelligibly asked about reality as a whole (including God); teleological explanation, pushed far enough, either reaches an unexplained Creator or becomes an impious/unmeaning question, and mechanistic explanation, pushed far enough, likewise reaches an uncaused first cause.
competing_positions: Teleological explanation, associated by Russell with Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell says the mechanistic question is the one that leads to scientific knowledge, implicitly connecting the atomists to the method of modern science, while the teleological question dominated European thought until the Renaissance.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Russell notes teleological explanation, pressed to its limit, usually terminates in a Creator or Artificer, and that asking what purpose the Creator serves is both impious and unmeaning.

core_concepts.name: Determinism and the rejection of chance
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Although people accused the atomists of saying everything happens by random chance, they actually believed the opposite: that everything happens by strict natural law and necessity, with nothing uncaused.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The atomists' doctrine, contrary to a common ancient misreading, that all events occur of necessity in accordance with natural law; Leucippus is quoted as saying 'Naught happens for nothing, but everything from a ground and of necessity,' and Democritus explicitly denied that anything happens by chance.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It positions the atomists as strict determinists whose only unexplained element is the original motion of the atoms, which Russell argues is not a defect since any causal chain must have an arbitrary, uncaused starting point.
objections: Aristotle and others reproached the atomists for not explaining the original motion of the atoms, which Russell defends as no real defect, since 'causation must start from something, and wherever it starts no cause can be assigned for the initial datum.'
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Rules out 'Providence' or divine purpose as governing events.

core_concepts.name: Perception and the primary/secondary quality distinction
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Democritus thought some qualities we perceive, like warmth, taste, and colour, are not really properties of objects themselves but are produced by our sense organs, while other qualities, like weight, density, and hardness, really do belong to the object.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Democritus's distinction between perception of the senses (dependent partly on the perceiver's sense-organs and therefore potentially deceptive) and perception of the understanding (dependent only on the object perceived); qualities like warmth, taste, and colour belong to the former and are not truly in the object, while qualities like weight, density, and hardness are truly in the object.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell explicitly compares this to Locke's later primary/secondary quality distinction, making Democritus an ancient anticipation of an idea central to early modern epistemology.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Part of Democritus's broader materialist account of perception and thought as physical processes.
examples: Warmth, taste, and colour as sense-dependent, not really in the object
Weight, density, and hardness as really in the object
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Explicitly likened by Russell to John Locke's similar distinction.

core_concepts.name: Democritus's ethics of cheerfulness
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Democritus thought the goal of life is cheerfulness, best achieved through moderation and culture; he disliked violence, passion, and (in his view) the loss of self-control involved in sex, and valued friendship and democracy while thinking little of women and not wanting children.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Democritus's ethical position that cheerfulness (euthymia) is the goal of life, to be attained through moderation and culture, combined with a dislike of violent passion, disapproval of sexual pleasure as an overwhelming of consciousness, valuing of friendship, low estimation of women, avoidance of children (whose education would interfere with philosophy), and preference for democracy even amid poverty over prosperity under despots.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell explicitly likens Democritus to Jeremy Bentham in both his ethical outlook and his love of what the Greeks called democracy, making him a notable ancient forerunner of later utilitarian and liberal-democratic sensibilities.
examples: Democritus's saying that poverty in a democracy is preferable to prosperity under despots, as freedom is to slavery
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Compared by Russell to Jeremy Bentham.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Rejected popular religion; valued democratic government despite its material costs.

arguments.title: Leucippus's reconciliation of Parmenides and the fact of motion
premises: Motion, change, and plurality are undeniable facts of sense-experience.
Parmenides is correct that there could be no motion in a true plenum (a space completely full of being, with no not-being).
Therefore, for motion to be possible, there must be a void (empty space, or not-being) as well as a plenum of many indivisible, unchanging bodies (atoms).
arguments.conclusion: Reality consists of an infinite number of indivisible atoms (each internally a 'Parmenidean One') moving, colliding, combining, and separating within an infinite void; coming-to-be and passing-away are just the coming-together and separating of atoms, not real generation or destruction of substance.
arguments.explanation: Russell frames this as Leucippus's central move: rather than choosing between Parmenides's unchanging One and the obvious plurality and motion of ordinary experience, he grants Parmenides that each individual atom is internally unified and unchanging (like Parmenides's Being) while positing many such atoms plus a void, so motion and plurality become possible at the level of arrangement even though nothing is truly created or destroyed at the level of the atoms themselves.
objections: Parmenides's arguments against not-being seem, Russell says, 'logically irrefutable' against the void, and the atomists never actually answered them; they simply proclaimed they would ignore the argument because motion is a fact of experience.

It was widely believed there could be no motion in a plenum at all; Russell says this common assumption was itself mistaken, since cyclic motion in an eternally existing plenum is possible, though motion could never begin in a plenum.
implications: Establishes atomism as, in Russell's view, the most scientifically minded ancient response to the problem of change.
Opens the long historical debate over the nature of space that Russell traces through Aristotle, Newton, Descartes, Leibniz, and Einstein.

arguments.title: Russell's defense of the atomists against the charge that they left the atoms' original motion unexplained
premises: Aristotle and other critics fault the atomists for not accounting for the origin of the atoms' motion.
Any causal chain of explanation must begin somewhere.
Wherever a causal chain begins, no further cause can be assigned for that initial starting point, whether the starting point is atoms in motion or a Creator.
arguments.conclusion: It is no defect in atomist theory that the original movement of the atoms is left unaccounted for, since every causal or teleological account, including theistic ones, must have an equally unexplained starting point.
arguments.explanation: Russell generalizes the point: even attributing the world to a Creator does not solve the problem, since the Creator Himself would then be unaccounted for. This is used to defend the atomists against what Russell treats as an unfair asymmetry in ancient and later criticism of their system.
implications: Undercuts the objection that mechanistic explanation is inherently less complete than teleological explanation, since both terminate in an arbitrary, uncaused beginning.

key_distinctions: Atoms (physically indivisible units) versus the void (empty space) in which they move
Mechanistic explanation (prior cause) versus teleological explanation (final cause/purpose)
Perception 'of the senses' (deceptive, sense-organ-dependent) versus perception 'of the understanding' (dependent only on the object) in Democritus
Chance versus necessity: the atomists were strict determinists, not believers in random chance
Absolute space (Newton) versus space as extension of matter (Descartes) versus space as a system of relations (Leibniz)
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: The atomists are presented as directly answering Parmenides (whose logic against not-being and against real change they take seriously) and as mediating between Parmenides's monism and Empedocles's pluralism; Leucippus was 'much influenced by Parmenides and Zeno.' Their explanation of vortex-formation is explicitly contrasted with Anaxagoras's appeal to mind, covered in the previous chapter.
connections_to_later_philosophers: Epicurus later adopted and (in Russell's judgment) somewhat degraded the theory by assuming atoms were originally falling under weight. The problem of the void/space is traced forward through Aristotle, Newton (absolute space), Descartes (plenum), Leibniz (relational space, vindicated by Einstein), and into modern physics, where matter is treated as 'a way of grouping events' rather than unchanging substance. Democritus's primary/secondary quality distinction anticipates Locke, and his ethics of cheerfulness and love of democracy is compared to Jeremy Bentham.
political_social_context: Democritus's preference for 'poverty in a democracy' over 'prosperity under despots' reflects fifth-century Greek debates over forms of government; his cool reception in Athens (in contrast to Protagoras's warm welcome) is noted by Russell as a biographical detail.
religion_science_culture_context: The atomists rejected popular religion and any 'Providence' governing the cosmos; Democritus was a materialist who held the soul itself is composed of atoms and thought is a physical process. Russell treats the atomic theory as strikingly close to modern scientific atomism, though arrived at without the chemical evidence that later vindicated it.
russell_presentation: Russell treats Leucippus and Democritus together as the founders of a single system, crediting Leucippus with its fundamental ideas and Democritus with their detailed elaboration. He reconstructs their theory of atoms and the void as an attempt to reconcile Parmenides's logic (that there can be no real coming-to-be, passing-away, or void) with the observed facts of motion and plurality, conceding that the atomists never logically refuted Parmenides's argument against the void but simply insisted on it as required by experience. Russell defends them against the standard ancient charge of leaving atomic motion unaccounted for, arguing any causal or theistic account faces the identical problem of an unexplained starting point. He uses the atomists' void/space problem to launch an extended historical survey (Aristotle, Newton, Descartes, Leibniz, Einstein) concluding that Einstein's physics vindicates Leibniz's relational view of space over Newton's absolute space, even though Russell judges the Newtonian view to be the strict logical descendant of the atomists' own position. Russell praises the atomists' commitment to mechanistic over teleological explanation as scientifically fruitful and contrasts it favorably with the purpose-driven thought of Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle, which he says 'led science up a blind alley' until the Renaissance. He details Democritus's materialist cosmology (many worlds, atomic vortices), his likening of warmth/taste/colour to sense-dependent qualities (compared to Locke) as against 'really' objective qualities like weight and hardness, and his ethics of cheerfulness, moderation, friendship, and preference for democracy, which Russell compares to Jeremy Bentham. Russell closes the chapter (and the pre-Socratic sequence) by calling Democritus 'the last of the Greek philosophers to be free from a certain fault which vitiated all later ancient and medieval thought': an undue emphasis on man relative to the universe, a decline he traces through the Sophists' scepticism, Socrates's turn to ethics, Plato's rejection of the sensory world, and Aristotle's belief in purpose as fundamental to science.
critical_context: Scholarly dispute noted explicitly by Russell: commentators disagree about the character of the atoms' original motion. Zeller holds that the atoms were thought of as originally falling, with heavier atoms overtaking lighter ones (the view Epicurus later adopted); Russell instead favors, following Burnet and (for Leucippus) Bailey, the view that atoms moved originally at random, like motes in a sunbeam or gas particles in the modern kinetic theory, calling this 'a much more intelligent view.' Russell also flags disagreement over whether Leucippus had any answer at all to the Parmenidean argument against the void: he states the atomists 'merely proclaimed that they proposed to ignore it,' but notes in a footnote that Bailey argues Leucippus did have a subtle answer, distinguishing the void as something real but not corporeal, a reading Burnet also supports. These are presented by Russell as live, labeled interpretive disagreements among modern scholars of the atomists (Zeller, Burnet, Bailey), not as settled fact.
key_takeaways: Leucippus and Democritus founded atomism, holding that everything consists of indestructible, physically indivisible atoms moving through an empty void, differing only in shape and size.

Atomism was devised to reconcile Parmenides's logical arguments against change and the void with the observed fact of motion; the atomists conceded they had no logical refutation of Parmenides and simply insisted on the void as an empirical necessity.

The atomists were strict determinists, not believers in chance: everything happens of necessity according to natural law, though the atoms' original motion is left unexplained (which Russell defends as unavoidable in any causal system).

Russell credits the atomists with favoring mechanistic explanation (prior causes) over teleological explanation (purposes), a choice he says anticipates the method of modern science, unlike the purpose-driven philosophy of Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle that followed.

Democritus distinguished sense-dependent qualities (warmth, taste, colour) from truly objective qualities (weight, density, hardness), anticipating Locke's primary/secondary quality distinction; his ethics prized cheerfulness, moderation, friendship, and democracy.

Russell traces the ancient dispute over the void into modern physics and philosophy of space (Newton's absolute space, Descartes's plenum, Leibniz's relational space, vindicated by Einstein), presenting atomism as the ancient theory most akin to modern science.
study_notes:
This chapter has two intertwined layers that are worth studying separately before combining them. The first layer is straightforwardly historical and doctrinal: who Leucippus and Democritus were, and what the atomic theory actually claimed (indivisible, indestructible atoms of differing shape and size, moving through a void, combining and separating to produce the appearance of coming-to-be and passing-away, with vortices of colliding atoms generating multiple, mortal worlds). Pay attention to how carefully Russell separates what belongs to the theory from what belongs to Democritus's further elaboration (cosmology, biology, perception, ethics), since the two men are historically difficult to disentangle.

The second layer is Russell's own philosophical commentary, which is unusually extensive in this chapter and deserves to be studied as a distinct strand. Russell uses the atomists' problem, motion requires a void, but Parmenides seems to show a void cannot exist, as a springboard for a compressed history of the philosophy of space running from Aristotle through Newton, Descartes, and Leibniz to Einstein. Be careful to keep this material properly labeled: it is Russell's own exposition and argument (so it belongs with his Layer 1 presentation of the chapter, not a later scholarly addition), even though it ranges far beyond antiquity. The key claims to retain are: (1) Newton's absolute space is presented as the strict logical heir of the atomists' own commitments; (2) Leibniz's rival view, that space is merely a system of relations, is said to have been vindicated by Einstein; and (3) modern physics has in any case abandoned both empty space and unchanging matter in favor of treating even matter as patterns of events.

Finally, connect the mechanistic-versus-teleological distinction to the chapter's closing judgment. Russell regards the atomists' choice to ask only 'what caused this?' rather than 'what purpose does this serve?' as historically decisive and scientifically fruitful, and uses it to explain why he treats Democritus as the last pre-Socratic thinker before what he sees as a long decline, running through the Sophists' scepticism, Socratic ethics, Platonic other-worldliness, and Aristotelian teleology, that in his view delayed the return of a genuinely scientific outlook until the Renaissance. This closing judgment is explicitly evaluative on Russell's part and worth flagging as such when you encounter it.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The smallest possible piece of matter, according to the atomists: something so small it cannot be physically split any further.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: In Leucippus and Democritus's theory, a physically (though not geometrically) indivisible, indestructible unit of matter, differing from other atoms only in shape and size, moving eternally through the void.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Truly empty space, with nothing at all in it, which the atomists said must exist so that atoms have room to move.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Empty space, treated by the atomists as a form of not-being that nonetheless must exist to make motion possible, in direct defiance of Parmenides's argument that not-being cannot be said to exist.
related_concepts: The void as a response to Parmenides

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A universe completely full of matter, with no empty space anywhere.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: A space entirely filled with being/matter, with no void; both Parmenides's monism and Descartes's later theory of extension imply a plenum, in which, it was widely assumed in antiquity, motion is impossible.
related_concepts: The void as a response to Parmenides

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Explaining an event by what caused it beforehand, rather than by what purpose it serves.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: An explanation that answers the question 'what earlier circumstances caused this event,' as opposed to a teleological explanation, which answers 'what purpose did this event serve'; the method Russell credits the atomists with pioneering.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Explaining something by the purpose or goal it serves, rather than by what caused it.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: An explanation by final cause: an event in the future for the sake of which an occurrence takes place; Russell associates this method with Socrates, Plato, and especially Aristotle, in contrast to the atomists' mechanistic method.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The idea that some properties of things (like weight or hardness) are really in the object, while others (like colour, taste, or warmth) only exist because of how our senses respond.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Democritus's distinction between qualities 'of the understanding,' held to be genuinely in the object (weight, density, hardness), and qualities 'of the senses,' held to depend on the perceiver's sense-organs and therefore to be potentially deceptive (warmth, taste, colour); explicitly compared by Russell to Locke's later distinction.
related_concepts: Perception and the primary/secondary quality distinction

questions.prompt: What problem were Leucippus and Democritus's atomic theory designed to solve?
questions.answer: How to reconcile Parmenides's argument that reality is one, unchanging, and admits no not-being (void) with the plain fact of motion, change, and plurality; atomism mediates between Parmenides's monism and Empedocles's pluralism.
questions.explanation: Russell frames atomism as arising directly out of this tension between Parmenidean logic and ordinary experience.

questions.prompt: Did the atomists logically refute Parmenides's argument against the void, according to Russell?
questions.answer: No. Russell says the atomists 'merely proclaimed that they proposed to ignore it, on the ground that motion is a fact of experience, and therefore there must be a void, however difficult it may be to conceive.'
questions.explanation: This shows the empirical, rather than purely logical, basis of the atomists' central postulate.

questions.prompt: Compare mechanistic and teleological explanation as Russell defines them, using his own baker/railway examples.
questions.answer: Mechanistic explanation answers 'what earlier circumstances caused this event?' Teleological explanation answers 'what purpose did this event serve?' Russell's examples: the baker makes bread because people will be hungry (teleological); railways are built because people will wish to travel (teleological). The atomists asked the mechanistic question instead and, in Russell's view, this choice is what led to genuine scientific knowledge.
questions.explanation: Understanding this distinction is essential to Russell's larger argument about why the atomists were scientifically ahead of their successors.

questions.prompt: According to Russell, why is it no defect in atomist theory that the original motion of the atoms is left unexplained?
questions.answer: Because every causal explanation must have an arbitrary starting point; wherever a causal chain begins, no cause can be assigned for that initial datum, and even attributing the world to a Creator leaves the Creator Himself unaccounted for.
questions.explanation: Russell uses this to defend the atomists against a common ancient and later criticism (made by Aristotle among others).

questions.prompt: Which modern philosopher's distinction between qualities does Russell say Democritus's view of perception resembles?
questions.answer: John Locke's distinction between primary and secondary qualities.
questions.explanation: Democritus held warmth, taste, and colour are not really in objects but produced by our senses, while weight, density, and hardness really are in objects, a view Russell explicitly likens to Locke.

questions.prompt: What did Democritus consider the goal of life, and by what means did he think it was best achieved?
questions.answer: Cheerfulness, best achieved through moderation and culture; he disliked violence and passion, disapproved of sex, valued friendship, and preferred democracy (even with poverty) to prosperity under despots.
questions.explanation: Russell likens this ethical outlook to Jeremy Bentham's.

questions.prompt: Whose view of space does Russell say Einstein's physics ultimately vindicated: Newton's or Leibniz's? Briefly explain the disagreement between them.
questions.answer: Leibniz's. Newton held space is an absolute substance, existing independently of matter, allowing a distinction between absolute and relative motion; Leibniz held space is merely a system of relations between things, with no substantial existence of its own. Russell says the controversy remained undecided until Einstein, whose theory 'conclusively gave the victory to Leibniz.'
questions.explanation: This is part of Russell's extended excursus tracing the atomists' void problem into modern physics.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct, in your own words, Leucippus's argument for accepting both atoms and the void despite Parmenides's objections.
questions.answer: Premise 1: motion and plurality are facts of experience. Premise 2: there can be no motion in a true plenum (a space entirely full, with no not-being). Conclusion: therefore a void must exist alongside a plurality of indivisible, unchanging atoms, even though this cannot be logically reconciled with Parmenides's argument that not-being (the void) cannot be said to exist.
questions.explanation: This question tests whether students can lay out the structure Russell attributes to Leucippus's reasoning, including its acknowledged logical weak point.

flashcards.front: Who are the two founders of ancient atomism?
Where was Leucippus from, and who influenced him?
flashcards.back: Miletus; he was influenced by Parmenides and Zeno.

flashcards.front: What did the atomists believe atoms were made of / how were they described?
flashcards.back: Physically (but not geometrically) indivisible, indestructible units, always in motion, differing in shape and size, moving through an infinite void.

flashcards.front: What problem does atomism try to solve, according to Russell?
flashcards.back: How to reconcile Parmenides's argument against change and the void with the observed fact of motion, mediating between Parmenides's monism and Empedocles's pluralism.

flashcards.front: Did the atomists logically refute Parmenides's argument against the void?
flashcards.back: No; Russell says they simply insisted on the void as required by the fact of motion, without answering the logical objection.

flashcards.front: Were the atomists believers in chance, or in strict determinism?
flashcards.back: Strict determinism; Democritus explicitly denied that anything happens by chance, and Leucippus said everything happens 'from a ground and of necessity.'

flashcards.front: What is the mechanistic question, as Russell defines it?
flashcards.back: What earlier circumstances caused this event?

flashcards.front: What is the teleological question, as Russell defines it?
flashcards.back: What purpose did this event serve?

flashcards.front: Which kind of explanation (mechanistic or teleological) does Russell say the atomists used, and which led to scientific knowledge?
flashcards.back: The atomists used mechanistic explanation; Russell says experience has shown the mechanistic question, not the teleological one, leads to scientific knowledge.

flashcards.front: Why, according to Russell, is it not a defect that the atomists left the atoms' original motion unexplained?
flashcards.back: Because any causal chain must have an arbitrary, uncaused starting point, whether that starting point is atoms in motion or a Creator.

flashcards.front: What did Democritus think about warmth, taste, and colour versus weight, density, and hardness?
flashcards.back: Warmth, taste, and colour are not really in the object but produced by our senses; weight, density, and hardness really are in the object, similar to Locke's later distinction.

flashcards.front: What did Democritus consider the goal of life?
flashcards.back: Cheerfulness, achieved through moderation and culture.

flashcards.front: Which modern political thinker does Russell compare Democritus to?
flashcards.back: Jeremy Bentham, both in ethics and in love of democracy.

flashcards.front: Whose theory of space did Einstein's physics ultimately vindicate: Newton's absolute space or Leibniz's relational space?
What did Democritus say happened when he first visited Athens?
flashcards.back: 'I went to Athens, and no one knew me,' unlike Protagoras, who was received enthusiastically.

quiz.prompt: Who are credited as the two founders of ancient atomism?
quiz.explanation: Leucippus and Democritus are the founders of the atomic theory of matter discussed in this chapter.

quiz.prompt: According to the atomists' theory, what are atoms moving through?
quiz.explanation: Atoms move through the void, empty space, which the atomists insisted must exist for motion to be possible.

quiz.prompt: The atomists logically refuted Parmenides's argument that the void (not-being) cannot exist.
quiz.explanation: False: Russell says they never answered the argument, but simply insisted on the void because motion is a fact of experience.
quiz.related_concept: The void as a response to Parmenides

quiz.prompt: Contrary to a common ancient accusation, what did the atomists actually believe about chance and necessity?
options: That everything happens by pure chance
That they were strict determinists: everything happens of necessity according to natural law
That chance and necessity are the same thing
That the gods control all events
quiz.explanation: Russell stresses that, despite being reproached for attributing everything to chance, the atomists were strict determinists who denied anything happens by chance.
quiz.related_concept: Determinism and the rejection of chance

quiz.prompt: Which question does Russell say the atomists asked, leading (in his view) to genuine scientific knowledge?
options: The teleological question: what purpose does this serve?
The mechanistic question: what earlier circumstances caused this event?
The theological question: what does God intend?
The ethical question: is this good or bad?
quiz.explanation: Russell credits the atomists with asking the mechanistic rather than the teleological question, and says experience shows this is the question that leads to scientific knowledge.

quiz.prompt: Russell says it is no defect in atomist theory that the atoms' original motion is left unexplained, because every causal chain must have an ______ starting point.
quiz.explanation: Russell argues that wherever a causal explanation begins, no cause can be given for that initial starting point, whether atoms or a Creator.
quiz.related_concept: Determinism and the rejection of chance

quiz.prompt: According to Democritus, which of these qualities is genuinely in the object rather than produced by our senses?
quiz.explanation: Democritus held that weight, density, and hardness are really in objects, while warmth, taste, and colour are produced by our sense-organs, a view Russell compares to Locke's.
quiz.related_concept: Perception and the primary/secondary quality distinction

quiz.prompt: According to Russell, whose theory of space did Einstein's physics ultimately vindicate?
options: Leibniz's theory that space is a system of relations
quiz.explanation: Russell states that the Newton-Leibniz controversy over space 'remained undecided until the time of Einstein, whose theory conclusively gave the victory to Leibniz.'
quiz.related_concept: The void as a response to Parmenides

quiz.prompt: Russell describes Democritus's ethical outlook, including his valuing of moderation, friendship, and democracy, as similar to that of Jeremy Bentham.
quiz.explanation: True: Russell explicitly compares Democritus to Bentham in ethics and in his love of democracy.

essay_prompts.prompt: Analyze Russell's distinction between mechanistic and teleological explanation as applied to the atomists. Why does he consider the atomists' choice of the mechanistic question historically and scientifically significant, and what limitation does he place on both kinds of explanation when applied to reality 'as a whole'?
rubric: Accurate statement of the mechanistic/teleological distinction using Russell's own examples
Clear explanation of why Russell favors the mechanistic approach for scientific purposes
Accurate account of Russell's limitation argument (neither explanation applies to the whole of reality, including God)
Original critical engagement with the strength of Russell's argument

essay_prompts.prompt: Compare the atomists' response to Parmenides with Anaxagoras's response (from the previous chapter). How does each attempt to reconcile the reality of change and motion with Parmenidean logic, and which does Russell present as the more 'advanced' or scientific solution?
rubric: Accurate account of Anaxagoras's universal-mixture/mind theory
Accurate account of the atomists' atoms-and-void theory
Clear comparison of how each handles the problem of change
Reference to Russell's explicit judgment that the atomists' mechanical account of vortex-formation is 'an advance' over Anaxagoras's appeal to mind

essay_prompts.prompt: Evaluate Russell's defense of the atomists against the charge that they failed to explain the original motion of the atoms. Is his argument, that any causal (or theistic) explanation must have an arbitrary starting point, a fully satisfying response to their ancient critics?
rubric: Accurate statement of the original criticism (attributed to Aristotle and others)
Consideration of possible objections to Russell's counter-argument
